chunks: Why puncturing a LiPo is dangerous. The question: Why is it so dangerous to puncture LiPos?
Puncturing a LiPo is dangerous because it creates a short circuit inside the cell itself. The object pushes through the thin layers and connects the two electrodes.
The cell's energy then flows through that tiny spot as heat, which can trigger thermal runaway: venting, fire and toxic fumes. The danger can also show up hours later.
Imagine a stack of metal foils separated by sheets of tissue paper. Push a nail through the stack and it touches foils that were meant to stay apart.
Electricity now has a direct path through the nail, right in the middle of the stack. Nothing outside the stack can stop it, because the connection is on the inside.
A fuse on the outside wires cannot see it.
A pouch cell is a sandwich of thin layers.
The nail connects the aluminium and copper sides through the separator, so the stored energy discharges through the nail and the layers around it.
The red path never leaves the pouch, so nothing connected to the external terminals can interrupt it.
Internal short circuit: the two electrodes connected inside the cell ("LiPo cell materials").
Separator: the thin film, only some tens of micrometers thick, that keeps the electrodes apart. Pouch cell: a cell in a soft foil bag with no rigid case ("What LiPo stands for").
Thermal runaway: self-feeding heating that ends in venting and fire ("Dangers of lithium batteries and prevention").
External protection: fuses and protection circuits in the outside wiring. They cannot interrupt an inside short.
Take a full cell at 4. 2 volts with 50 milliohms of internal resistance. A nail makes a short of 100 milliohms. The current is 4. 2 over (0. 05 plus 0. 1) equals 28 amps.
The heat in the short is about 28 squared times 0. 1 equals 78 watts, packed into a spot about a millimeter across.
That melts the separator around it, which makes the short larger, and it starts the heating loop. That is the whole idea.
"A LiPo is a thin stack of electrodes separated by a micron-scale separator in a soft foil pouch.
A puncture bridges the electrodes, creating an internal short: the cell's energy dumps through a tiny spot, heating it fast, melting the separator and starting thermal runaway.
Air and moisture entering make it worse.
No protection circuit or fuse can help because the short is inside the cell, and damage can be delayed, so punctured or crushed cells should be treated as dangerous."
